title: The Criminal Father of Criminology
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Eugène-François Vidocq, the early 19th-century Paris criminal turned police informant who founded the Sûreté's Security Brigade and later a private detective agency, and is often called the father of criminology. The episode covers his rowdy youth, army desertion, life as a forger and prison escapee (including the galley prison, or bagno), his deal to become an informant, the all-ex-convict Security Brigade, his pioneering forensic techniques (ballistics, footprint casts, a criminal card index, a treatise on thieves' language), the police rivalry and his disputed conviction for false imprisonment, his detective agency, and his influence on Victor Hugo, Balzac, Poe and later detective fiction. The episode ends with a listener email about the Hyatt Regency Skywalk disaster.

entities.name: The Murders in the Rue Morgue

segments.title: Introduction to Vidocq
segments.summary: Hosts introduce Eugène-François Vidocq, known as the father of criminology, and his role as a reformed criminal who became a top cop in Paris.

segments.title: Early life and army desertion
segments.summary: Vidocq's youthful delinquency, including stealing from his parents, running away to the circus, working for a Punch and Judy show, being sent to the army, and deserting after a duel challenge. He then joined the Rolling Army under an alias.

segments.title: Paris crime and early criminal career
segments.summary: Post-Revolution Paris was overrun with crime because police were drawn away and the regime changed repeatedly. Vidocq became a forger and schemer in Paris, in and out of prison.

segments.title: Bagno prison and escapes
segments.summary: Vidocq forged release papers for a bread thief, was sentenced to eight years, sent to the bagno hard-labor prison, and escaped twice, once disguised as a nun.

segments.title: Becoming a police informant
segments.summary: In 1809 Vidocq offered to inform for police from prison, working two years as an informant. He was then released unofficially by police chief Jean Henry and became an undercover agent, a new practice. Debate over whether his motives were self-serving or a genuine change of heart.

segments.title: Security Brigade
segments.summary: In 1812 Vidocq became chief of the Sûreté's Security Brigade, staffed by ex-convicts. Napoleon made it a state police force. Its reported arrest numbers and famous cases, including a stagecoach shootout, drew rivalry from the regular police.

segments.title: Forensic innovations
segments.summary: Vidocq is credited with early ballistics comparison in the Darci murder case, footprint casting with plaster, an attempted fingerprinting idea, and a card-index criminal database with handwriting samples.

segments.title: Criminal psychology and memoirs
segments.summary: Vidocq wrote a treatise on thieves' language and mores, a study of the criminal mind. His memoirs were reportedly ghostwritten and flourished with self-promotion. His men were skilled at disguise.

segments.title: Controversies and detective agency
segments.summary: Police accused Vidocq of illegal activity, mostly unproven. He resigned after a Security Brigade agent was convicted, was brought back, then founded the world's first private detective agency. A later case led to his conviction for false imprisonment, which was overturned on appeal, and he closed the agency.

segments.title: Legacy in literature and detective fiction
segments.summary: Vidocq inspired Victor Hugo's Les Misérables characters and Balzac's Vautrin, Edgar Allan Poe's Dupin, and Gaboriau's Lecoq, with Sherlock Holmes linked to Lecoq. The Vidocq Society in Philadelphia is named after him.

segments.title: Listener mail: Hyatt Regency Skywalk disaster
segments.summary: A physician who was a resident in Kansas City recalls the Skywalk disaster, a canceled mass-disaster drill, and that his sons learned about it in engineering classes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give the feedback email address; sign-off.
